phrases: Why is every window on every plane you've ever flown in round?
Because in the early nineteen-fifties, the world's first jet airliner kept tearing open in the sky.
In less than a year, three of them broke up in the air.
The killer was hiding in the corners.
This is the de Havilland Comet.
In nineteen fifty-two, the Comet became the first jet airliner to carry paying passengers.
It cruised up above the weather, at around thirty-five thousand feet, far faster than any propeller airliner.
Smooth, quiet, and sleek, with big windows to watch the clouds go by.
But up there, the air is far too thin to breathe.
So the cabin had to be pressurised.
Air is pumped into the cabin until it feels like being at about eight thousand feet, even though the plane is flying four times higher.
So the air inside pushes outward on the skin.
More than five tonnes on every square metre.
On every flight, the fuselage swells a tiny bit as it climbs, and relaxes as it lands.
Like a balloon, breathing in and out.
Once is fine.
But thousands of times?
Bend a paper clip once, and nothing happens.
Bend it back and forth, and it snaps.
Engineers call that metal fatigue.
It doesn't need a big force. Just a smaller one, repeated again and again, until a tiny crack starts to grow.
And cracks love one place more than any other.
Sharp corners.
Picture the stress in the skin as lines of force, flowing around a hole.
Around a round hole, they bend smoothly, and the load is shared.
But at a sharp corner, they have to squeeze around a tight turn.
The stress piles up right at the tip, several times higher than in the rest of the skin.
Engineers call this a stress concentration.
And a tiny crack at a corner is an even sharper corner, so once it starts, it grows faster and faster.
The Comet's skin was thin, and its openings had tight, almost square corners.
Windows, hatches, and a small window in the roof for a navigation antenna.
And many rivet holes were punched, not drilled, leaving tiny flaws right where the stress was highest.
In May, nineteen fifty-three, a Comet broke up in a violent storm near Calcutta.
In January, nineteen fifty-four, another came apart at about twenty-seven thousand feet, over the sea near the island of Elba.
The Comets were grounded, checked over, and cleared to fly again.
Just two weeks later, a third Comet broke up over the sea near Naples.
Nobody on any of the three flights survived.
So engineers at Farnborough, in England, did something new.
They put a whole Comet fuselage into a giant tank of water.
Why water?
Because if it burst, water wouldn't explode outward like compressed air.
Then they pumped it up and let it down, again and again, one fake flight every few minutes.
After about three thousand flights, real and simulated, the skin split open, from a crack at the corner of an opening.
Wreckage lifted from the sea near Elba told the same story.
The crack had started at a corner of that little roof window.
The answer changed every airliner that came after.
Openings got rounded corners, so the stress can flow smoothly around them.
The Comet came back as the Comet four, with thicker skin and rounded windows.
Designers added straps that stop a crack from running, so one crack can't tear open the whole cabin.
And new airliners are tested by flexing a full airframe for far more flights than they will ever fly.
Today, airliner windows are small and rounded, and the skin around each one is made thicker, to carry the load around the hole.
In nineteen fifty-eight, a Comet four flew the first transatlantic jet service with passengers.
So the next time you look out of a round plane window, that curve is a lesson, learned the hard way.
